items.title: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
items.summary: Every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique apart from the order of factors.
steps: Divide the number by the smallest prime that divides it.
Continue factoring each composite quotient until every factor is prime.
Arrange the prime factors in non-decreasing order.
Uniqueness follows from Euclid's lemma: if a prime divides a product, it divides at least one factor.
items.examTip: Use prime factorisation to find HCF and LCM; show the factor tree or division steps.

items.title: Euclid's Division Lemma
items.summary: For positive integers a and b, there exist unique integers q and r such that a = bq + r, where 0 ≤ r < b.
steps: Identify the dividend a and divisor b.
Write a = bq + r.
Check that the remainder is non-negative and smaller than the divisor.

items.title: HCF–LCM relationship
items.formula: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b
items.summary: For two positive integers, the product of their HCF and LCM equals the product of the integers.

items.title: Relationship between zeroes and coefficients (quadratic)
items.summary: For p(x) = ax² + bx + c, with zeroes α and β: α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a.
steps: Factorise p(x) as a(x − α)(x − β).
Expand: a[x² − (α + β)x + αβ].
Compare coefficients with ax² + bx + c.
Equate x-coefficients and constant terms to obtain the relationships.
items.examTip: State the degree and leading coefficient before applying the relationships.

items.title: Division algorithm for polynomials
items.formula: p(x) = g(x)q(x) + r(x), where r(x) = 0 or degree r(x) < degree g(x)
items.summary: Dividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder.

items.title: Number of zeroes
items.summary: The number of zeroes of a polynomial is at most its degree. A quadratic can have at most two real zeroes.
items.diagramAlt: Graph showing zeroes of a quadratic polynomial.

chapters.subject: mathematics
chapters.chapterTitle: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

items.title: Consistency conditions
items.summary: For a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0 and a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0, the ratios determine the number of solutions.
steps: Unique solution: a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂; the lines intersect.
No solution: a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂; the lines are parallel.
Infinitely many solutions: a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂; the lines coincide.
items.diagramAlt: Graph of two intersecting linear equations.

items.title: Cross-multiplication method
items.summary: Use when the denominator conditions are satisfied.

items.title: Quadratic formula
items.summary: Solution of ax² + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0.
steps: Divide the equation by a.
Move the constant term to the right.
Complete the square by adding b²/(4a²) to both sides.
Take square roots and isolate x to obtain the quadratic formula.
items.examTip: The discriminant D = b² − 4ac determines the nature of roots.

items.title: Nature of roots
items.formula: D > 0: two distinct real roots · D = 0: equal real roots · D < 0: no real roots
items.summary: Check the discriminant before solving when only the nature of roots is asked.

items.title: nth term
items.summary: a is the first term, d is the common difference and n is the term number.

items.title: Sum of first n terms
items.summary: Pair the first and last terms to derive the AP sum.
steps: Write Sₙ = a + (a+d) + … + l.
Reverse the order: Sₙ = l + (l−d) + … + a.
Add the two equations; each pair equals a + l.
Thus 2Sₙ = n(a+l), so Sₙ = n/2(a+l).
items.examTip: Use the first formula when d is known; use the second when the last term is known.

items.title: Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales)
items.summary: A line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides in the same ratio.
steps: In ΔABC, let D lie on AB and E on AC with DE ∥ BC.
Triangles ADE and BDE have equal altitude to AB, so their area ratio is AD:DB.
Similarly compare areas using the common altitude to AC.
Using the equal areas of triangles sharing base DE and parallel lines, obtain AD/DB = AE/EC.
items.diagramAlt: Triangle with a line parallel to its base.

items.title: Pythagoras theorem
items.summary: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides.
steps: Let ∠B = 90° in ΔABC.
Draw BD perpendicular to AC.
Use similarity of the smaller triangles with the original triangle.
Obtain AB² = AD·AC and BC² = DC·AC.
Add: AB² + BC² = AC(AD+DC) = AC².

items.title: Similarity criteria
items.summary: AAA (or AA), SSS and SAS similarity criteria. Corresponding sides of similar triangles are proportional.

items.title: Distance formula
items.summary: Distance between A(x₁,y₁) and B(x₂,y₂).

items.title: Section formula (internal division)
items.summary: If P divides AB in the ratio m:n.

items.title: Area of a triangle
items.summary: If area is zero, the three points are collinear.

items.title: Trigonometric ratios
items.formula: sin θ = P/H · cos θ = B/H · tan θ = P/B
items.summary: P = perpendicular, B = base, H = hypotenuse in a right triangle.

items.title: Fundamental identity
items.summary: Divide the Pythagorean relation P² + B² = H² by H².
steps: Start with P² + B² = H².
Divide every term by H².
Recognise P/H = sin θ and B/H = cos θ.
Therefore sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
items.examTip: Also derive 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

items.title: Angle of elevation and depression
items.summary: Angle of elevation is measured upward from the horizontal; angle of depression is measured downward from the horizontal.
items.diagramAlt: Right triangle used to model height and distance.

items.title: Height and distance setup
items.summary: Choose the right triangle, identify the angle, then select sin, cos or tan based on known and required sides.
steps: Draw and label the horizontal line and vertical height.
Mark the angle of elevation/depression.
Identify opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse.
Apply the appropriate ratio and include units.

items.title: Tangents from an external point
items.summary: The lengths of two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
steps: Let PA and PB be tangents from P, touching at A and B.
Join OA, OB and OP.
OA ⟂ PA and OB ⟂ PB (radius is perpendicular to tangent).
OA = OB (radii) and OP is common.
Right triangles OAP and OBP are congruent by RHS; hence PA = PB.
items.diagramAlt: Two equal tangents from an external point.

items.title: Tangent–radius property
items.summary: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.

items.title: Circle and sector formulae
items.formula: Circumference = 2πr · Area = πr² · Arc length = (θ/360°) × 2πr · Sector area = (θ/360°) × πr²
items.summary: θ is the central angle in degrees.

items.title: Segment area
items.formula: Minor segment area = sector area − area of triangle
items.summary: For a major segment, subtract the minor segment from the area of the full circle.

items.title: Cylinder
items.summary: r is radius and h is height.

items.title: Cone and sphere
items.formula: Cone: CSA = πrl, V = ⅓πr²h · Sphere: SA = 4πr², V = ⁴⁄₃πr³
items.summary: For a cone, l = √(r²+h²).

items.title: Combined solids
items.summary: For a combined solid, add the exposed surface areas only. For hollowing or melting, conserve volume.

items.title: Mean of grouped data
items.summary: xᵢ is class mark and fᵢ is frequency.

items.title: Median of grouped data
items.summary: l = lower boundary of median class; cf = cumulative frequency before it; f = its frequency; h = class width.

items.title: Mode of grouped data
items.summary: f₁ is modal-class frequency; f₀ previous class; f₂ succeeding class.

items.title: Classical probability
items.formula: P(E) = Number of outcomes favourable to E / Total number of equally likely outcomes

items.title: Complementary event
items.summary: An event and its complement are mutually exclusive and together cover the entire sample space.
steps: The sample space S is partitioned into E and Ē.
Therefore P(E) + P(Ē) = P(S).
Since P(S) = 1, P(Ē) = 1 − P(E).

items.title: Alveolus – gas exchange
labels: Oxygen diffuses into blood; carbon dioxide diffuses into alveolus

items.title: Double circulation
items.alt: Schematic of pulmonary and systemic circulation.
labels: Pulmonary circulation – heart to lungs and back
Systemic circulation – heart to body and back

items.title: Photosynthesis equation
items.summary: Carbon dioxide and water are converted into glucose and oxygen using light energy.

items.title: Reflex arc – pathway
labels: Sensory neuron carries impulse to spinal cord
items.examTip: A reflex action is rapid and automatic; the brain is informed but the spinal cord coordinates many reflexes.

items.title: Human reproductive system – key structures
labels: Male: testes produce sperm; vas deferens transports sperm; urethra carries semen
Female: ovaries release ova; oviduct is the usual site of fertilisation
Placenta enables exchange between maternal and foetal blood without direct mixing
items.examTip: Be able to distinguish fertilisation, implantation and gestation.

items.title: Asexual reproduction methods
facts: One cell divides into two; e.g. Amoeba
A small outgrowth develops; e.g. Hydra
Body breaks into pieces that grow; e.g. Spirogyra
Spores germinate under favourable conditions; e.g. Rhizopus
New plants arise from vegetative parts

items.title: Monohybrid cross – Mendel
items.summary: A cross between two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt × Tt) gives genotypes TT, Tt, Tt and tt.
facts: Expressed only when both alleles are recessive

items.title: Sex determination in humans
items.summary: Mother is XX; father is XY. The ovum always contributes X; sperm contributes X or Y. The sperm determines the chromosomal sex of the child.

items.title: Energy flow in a food chain
items.summary: Energy flows in one direction through trophic levels; only about 10% of energy is transferred to the next trophic level.

items.title: Ozone layer and biomagnification
items.summary: Ozone shields life from harmful UV radiation. Non-biodegradable pollutants can become more concentrated at higher trophic levels.

items.title: Concave and convex lens ray diagrams
items.alt: Ray diagram schematic used for image formation reference.
labels: Image position depends on object distance
items.examTip: Draw at least two standard rays and mark the image orientation and size.

items.title: Mirror and lens formulae
items.summary: Use the Cartesian sign convention consistently.

items.title: Magnification and power
items.formula: Mirror: m = −v/u · Lens: m = v/u · P = 1/f (f in metres)
items.summary: Power is measured in dioptres (D).

chapters.chapterTitle: The Human Eye and the Colourful World

items.title: Correction of hypermetropia
labels: Image would form behind retina without correction
Convex lens converges rays so image forms on retina

items.title: Defects of vision
facts: Distant objects unclear; corrected using concave lens
Nearby objects unclear; corrected using convex lens
Age-related loss of accommodation; bifocal/progressive correction may be used

items.title: Scattering and dispersion
items.summary: Shorter wavelengths scatter more strongly; white light disperses into its constituent colours through a prism.
items.alt: Prism dispersing white light into a spectrum.

items.title: Ohm's law
items.summary: At constant temperature, current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it.

items.title: Resistance combinations
items.summary: Series current is the same; parallel potential difference is the same.

items.title: Electric power and heating
items.formula: P = VI = I²R = V²/R · H = I²Rt
items.summary: Power is in watts; electrical energy may be measured in joules or kilowatt-hours.

items.title: Rules for magnetic fields
facts: Thumb points in current direction; curled fingers show magnetic field direction
Forefinger: field; middle finger: current; thumb: force
Field resembles that of a bar magnet; nearly uniform inside

items.title: Domestic electric circuit safety
items.summary: Live wire carries supply, neutral completes circuit, and earth wire provides a low-resistance path during leakage. Fuse/MCB protects against excess current.
